subject: 2026-11-15-extensions

findings.title: Hostile source or name on add and remove is not handled
quotes: copy it into `.nio/extensions` and record the URL and the fetched version
WHEN `nio extensions remove` is given an added extension's name THE SYSTEM SHALL delete it from `.nio/extensions`
findings.fix: add an FR and an AC for a safe name (no separators or `..`), no symlinks or paths escaping the folder, git URLs limited to safe transports, and a size limit.

sources.situation: a manifest named `../../x` makes add write outside `.nio/extensions`, and remove then deletes the wrong folder. An extension folder with a symlink to `~/.ssh` is copied with its target. A git URL such as `ext::sh -c ...` or one starting with `-` runs code at fetch, which breaks "runs none of its commands". Nothing rejects an oversized or duplicated manifest field, and AC-5 covers only a missing or malformed field. The fetch itself runs before the review that FR-37 relies on.

findings.reason: a cited ID or quote is not in the artefact

findings.title: Remove silently moves an effort past a step and its gate
quotes: an effort sitting at it moves on to the next stage
findings.fix: record a skipped-by-removal line and refuse or warn on remove while an effort is at the step or another extension depends on it. Add an AC for each case.

sources.situation: an effort is at the e2e step (or in `judging` on an extension gate, awaiting approval) and the extension is removed. The effort skips the step, its check and its jury with no history line, and AC-7 tests only the effort before its spot. Removing extension A also leaves extension B's step with `after` naming A's now-missing step. No AC says what happens then, since FR-11 checks `after` only at add time. A re-add (FR-4) that drops a step has the same effect.

findings.title: The misuse "hand-editing to skip a gate" is covered only for built-in gates
quotes: hand-editing a copied extension to skip a gate.
IF an extension in `.nio/extensions` breaks the add-only rule when the flow reads it
findings.fix: record a content hash at add and refuse to run when it differs. Alternatively, state that the commit is the only control and add an AC that the flow prints changed commands.

sources.situation: someone edits an added extension's manifest so its check command is `true`, drops its jury gate declaration, or changes a hook command. This is still add-only, so FR-21 does not fire. The e2e check or the extension gate is silently disabled, and the only record is a git diff. The record holds source and version but no hash, so the flow cannot notice a change after add.

findings.reason: FR-21 fires only on an add-only breach. UJ-1 lists "hand-editing a copied extension to skip a gate" as misuse. The record holds only source and version (FR-1, Key entities), so a check command changed to `true` or a dropped jury gate goes unnoticed.
findings.note: FR-38 and AC-41: a hash recorded at add; a hand-edited extension stops the flow until re-added

findings.title: The e2e check can be satisfied by fake tests
quotes: every such test fails on its assertions, not on setup
findings.fix: define how an assertion failure is told from other failures (the runner's assertion error class) and require the test to drive the app, such as a visit or a click, before asserting. Otherwise state the limit and leave it to the jury.

sources.situation: the tester writes `expect(true).toBe(false)` under a comment naming the AC. It cites its AC and fails on an assertion, so the check passes. A test that fails on a typo, a selector timeout, or a 500 page from a half-started app also counts as an assertion failure. UJ-4 lists "tests that fail because the app never started rather than because the feature is missing" as misuse, but AC-31 only separates a non-starting app. Nothing separates failing because the feature is missing from failing for any other reason.

findings.title: Auto mode: the misuse line contradicts FR-19
quotes: an effort under auto passes an extension gate that should go to the human
so the driver's `nio flow done` approves a passing extension gate as it does the spec, plan and tasks gates
findings.fix: decide the case. Either an extension gate always waits for the human under auto unless the maintainer opts in per extension, or the misuse line is dropped. Add an AC for the chosen case.

sources.situation: FR-19 makes the driver approve any passing extension gate under auto. UJ-2 names that as misuse, yet FR-19 requires it. AC-19 tests only "Given an extension step that the flow's stop rules send to the human", and no rule decides which extension gates those are. An extension author can declare a gate that guards something sensitive, and auto approves it without anyone looking. The only hook for a human stop is the existing stop rules, which the spec doesn't say apply to an extension.

findings.title: Add-refused table copies a manifest with a hook on an unknown event
quotes: and refuse a manifest hook on any other
| yes | no | yes | no | copied and recorded | [human] |
card or hook clashes (yes, no)
findings.fix: add a column "hook names a known event (yes, no)" to the Add refused table, with a refused row for "no", and make the copied row require "yes" in it.

sources.situation: a manifest with a valid field set, a built-in step not touched, a known `after` step, and a hook on `build-done`. FR-26 says the add is refused for a hook on an event NIO doesn't fire. The table's only hook column is "card or hook clashes", which this case doesn't hit, so the row "copied and recorded" applies and the add succeeds.

findings.reason: The Add refused table's row 4 outcome reads "refused, names the card or event". So the "card or hook clashes" column is meant to cover an unknown-event hook, and row 5 ("copied") needs "no" there. The column label is loose, but the table does not copy such a manifest.

findings.title: "Hook" is already the name of the git-hook command
quotes: **Hook**: a shell command run on a NIO event.
run each shell hook that added extensions register on it
findings.fix: pick a term for extension event hooks (for example "event hook") and add it to the glossary with "Never 'hook' alone, that is `nio hooks`"; or state in the glossary that the spec's "hook" is not the git hook of `nio hooks`.

sources.situation: a maintainer reads "hook" in the spec and in `nio hooks`. In the pack, D-261024-jpst records that git hooks are "installed by nio hooks". Two different things share one word, and the glossary doesn't say which "hook" is meant.

findings.reason: The Glossary defines "Hook" with only "Never callback" and says nothing about `nio hooks`, which is the git-hook command in this repo. The same word names two different things.
findings.note: Glossary: Hook is not the git hooks of nio hooks; say event hook where both could be meant

findings.title: FR-19 puts auto stop rules into the flow, against the current decision that auto lives in the skills
quotes: WHILE an effort is under auto THE SYSTEM SHALL apply the same stop rules to extension steps and gates as to built-in ones
findings.fix: either state in FR-19 that the skills apply auto and the flow only reports the stop rule, or raise a change request against D-261115-cf65 and cite it in Decisions.

sources.situation: the pack's summary of cf65 says "auto lives in the existing skills". FR-19 makes the system (code) apply auto's stop rules to extension steps, so auto's behaviour would move into code, and the spec doesn't say it changes cf65. I can't read cf65's full text from the pack, so this may be a false alarm. If it isn't, a change request is needed before the spec passes.

findings.reason: D-261115-cf65 is about the full-auto driver loop and the fixer agent living in the existing jury and implement skills for that effort. It doesn't forbid the flow from applying stop rules to extension steps. FR-19 and the Decisions line "under the same stop rules" do not conflict with it.

findings.title: The spec never names the command that closes an epic
quotes: when the agent hands it back as done, then the epic stays open as with any failing test
Implementation is per epic, with the flow running the epic's tests at its end and no per-task red/green
findings.fix: name the command in AC-33 and the Decisions line, and make it the same one the decision names.

sources.situation: the current decision says the flow runs the epic's tests at its end, and the pack names that command as `nio flow finish`. AC-33 says "hands it back as done", which could mean `nio flow done` (used everywhere else in the spec for gates and extension steps) or the finish command. A tester can't tell which command must keep the epic open.

findings.note: a minor, accepted as the gate's risk under auto

findings.title: AC-3 doesn't cover the personal-folder copy that FR-3 says comes first
quotes: then the shipped e2e extension is copied into `.nio/extensions`
A name found in the person's `~/.nio/extensions` is copied from there first, and recorded with that folder as its source.
findings.fix: add to AC-3 the precondition "and no folder of that name is in `~/.nio/extensions`", and add an AC for the personal-folder case.

sources.situation: a person has `~/.nio/extensions/e2e` and runs `nio extensions add e2e`. FR-3 says that copy is used and its folder is recorded as the source. AC-3 says the shipped copy is copied and its source is recorded as shipped. A tester following AC-3 gets the other result.

findings.note: a minor, accepted as the gate's risk under auto

findings.title: Removing or replacing an extension leaves other extensions' `after` pointing at nothing
quotes: WHEN `nio extensions remove` is given an added extension's name THE SYSTEM SHALL delete it from `.nio/extensions`, so efforts that haven't reached its step no longer have it
IF a manifest's step names in `after` a step that is neither built in nor a step of an added extension THEN THE SYSTEM SHALL refuse the add and name that step.
findings.fix: state that remove or replace is refused (or that the flow refuses to move, as FR-21 does) while another added extension's `after` names a step it would take away, and say what the add table does with a step or card name that another added extension already uses.

sources.situation: extension B has a step with `after: a-step`, where `a-step` belongs to extension A. B was added while A was present, so FR-11 passed. The maintainer runs `nio extensions remove A`, or re-adds A (FR-4) in a version that drops or renames `a-step`. B's step now follows a step that exists nowhere. FR-11 only checks at add. FR-21 only covers the add-only rule. The spec doesn't say whether remove is refused, B's step is dropped, B's step is re-anchored, or the flow stops. The same hole exists for two extensions that declare the same step name or card name, since the "Add refused" table only checks a card clash with shipped cards.

findings.reason: FR-11 checks `after` only at add. FR-7 and FR-4 say nothing about another extension's step whose `after` names a step the removal or replacement takes away. The Add refused table checks a card clash only against shipped cards, so a clash with another added extension is open.
findings.note: FR-39 and AC-42: remove or replace refused while another extension's step follows a step it takes away; step or card name clashes with added extensions refused; add-refused table names step clashes

findings.title: A trigger rule has no outcome when its input doesn't exist
quotes: THE SYSTEM SHALL support the trigger rule "the plan touches files under a named path".
WHEN the flow reaches an extension step whose trigger rule doesn't apply to the effort THE SYSTEM SHALL skip it on the record
findings.fix: say whether an unevaluable trigger counts as "doesn't apply", as "applies", or refuses the add, or limit each trigger rule to the steps after which its input exists.

sources.situation: an author writes a step with `after: spec_jury` and the trigger "the plan touches files under `web/`". The plan doesn't exist when the step is reached. The state table sends `reached` to `active` or `skipped` and has no third result. The decision table has `trigger applies (yes, no)` and nothing for "can't be evaluated". AC-17 covers a check failing for missing inputs, but the trigger is evaluated first, so a missing plan is silently read as "doesn't apply". The step is then skipped on the record, which hides the author's mistake.

findings.reason: FR-12 and FR-13 and the decision table's `trigger applies (yes, no)` have no outcome for a trigger whose input (the plan) doesn't exist yet. FR-11 allows any known `after` step, and AC-17 covers only the check, not the trigger.
findings.note: FR-40 and AC-43: a trigger reading an input that doesn't exist yet at its after step is refused at add

findings.title: AC-3 contradicts the second sentence of FR-3
quotes: then the shipped e2e extension is copied into `.nio/extensions`.
A name found in the person's `~/.nio/extensions` is copied from there first, and recorded with that folder as its source.
findings.fix: make AC-3 conditional on there being no personal extension of that name, or change FR-3 so a shipped name always wins or always refuses on a clash.

sources.situation: the maintainer's `~/.nio/extensions` holds a folder named `e2e`. They run `nio extensions add e2e`. AC-3 says the shipped e2e extension is copied and recorded as shipped with NIO's version. FR-3 says the personal folder is copied and recorded with that folder as its source. The same input gives two different results, and the personal folder can stand in for the shipped one. AC-37's "no NIO code names the e2e extension" does not resolve it.

findings.note: a minor, accepted as the gate's risk under auto

findings.title: Removing an extension moves an effort off its step without the check or the gate
quotes: an effort sitting at it moves on to the next stage
move on only once the gate is approved as the built-in gates are
findings.fix: say in FR-7 that such an effort is recorded as skipped with "extension removed" as the reason, or that remove is refused while any effort sits at one of the extension's steps.

sources.situation: an effort is in `judging` at an extension step that declares a jury gate, waiting for approval. The maintainer removes the extension. FR-7 moves the effort to the next stage, so the gate was passed with no approval and no check, even though FR-23 says the effort moves on only once the gate is approved. Removal is a maintainer act and is reviewed in the commit, so this may be intended. But it is a second path past a gate, and the spec states no history line or reason for it. The "skipped on the record" form is only defined for trigger skips.

an effort is at the e2e step (or in `judging` on an extension gate, awaiting approval) and the extension is removed. The effort skips the step, its check and its jury with no history line, and AC-7 tests only the effort before its spot. Removing extension A also leaves extension B's step with `after` naming A's now-missing step. No AC says what happens then, since FR-11 checks `after` only at add time. A re-add (FR-4) that drops a step has the same effect.

findings.reason: FR-7 says an effort sitting at a removed step "moves on to the next stage", while FR-23 and the state table let an effort leave `judging` only on gate approval. Nothing in the spec (Decisions Q4 line, AC-7) names a history line or reason for this path, and the "skipped on the record" form is defined only for trigger skips (FR-12). The `after` dangling case is in the ledger as J-11.
findings.note: FR-7 and AC-44: remove refused while an effort sits at the step; past efforts keep stage and history

findings.title: "the flow's stop rules" for an extension gate are never named
quotes: THE SYSTEM SHALL apply the same stop rules to extension steps and gates as to built-in ones, so the driver's `nio flow done` approves a passing extension gate as it does the spec, plan and tasks gates.
Given an extension step that the flow's stop rules send to the human, when the effort is under auto, then the flow waits for the human
findings.fix: name the stop rules (or the rule that applies to extension gates) in FR-19, and say whether an extension gate counts as a spec-style gate or a pr-style gate for them.

sources.situation: FR-19 says the stop rules are the same and also says the driver approves a passing extension gate as it does the spec, plan and tasks gates. The pr gate is left out of that list. UJ-2 lists "an effort under auto passes an extension gate that should go to the human" as a misuse, but no rule says which extension gate that is. Built-in stop rules are keyed on the gate's own risk, and an extension gate has no entry in them. A maintainer can't tell from the spec whether an extension gate under auto with a `money` or `data-deletion` risk waits or passes, and AC-19 can't be written as a pass-or-fail case without that.

FR-19 makes the driver approve any passing extension gate under auto. UJ-2 names that as misuse, yet FR-19 requires it. AC-19 tests only "Given an extension step that the flow's stop rules send to the human", and no rule decides which extension gates those are. An extension author can declare a gate that guards something sensitive, and auto approves it without anyone looking. The only hook for a human stop is the existing stop rules, which the spec doesn't say apply to an extension.

findings.reason: FR-19 says "the same stop rules" but names none, and it says the driver approves a passing extension gate like the spec, plan and tasks gates. UJ-2 lists the same case as misuse, and AC-19 assumes a stop rule that sends an extension step to the human. Nothing in the spec says which extension gates that is, and Decisions only repeats "the same stop rules".
findings.note: FR-19, AC-19, UJ-2: an extension gate is treated as the spec, plan and tasks gates: approved by the driver once its jury approves, waits for the human when the jury outcome is human or a finding is held

findings.title: One spec carries an epic's worth of slices

The first extension, shipped and off by default, is a frontend e2e tester
findings.fix: split into an epic with slices (core add, list and remove with the flow step; cards and hooks with gates; the e2e

findings.reason: spec-scope: the spec was not split; the text still carries US-1 to US-6 and FR-35 to FR-41 as one spec. The

findings.title: AC-19 and FR-19 describe opposite outcomes under auto
quotes: then the flow waits for the human at that step as it does at built-in steps
so the driver's `nio flow done` approves a passing extension gate as it does the spec, plan and tasks gates
findings.fix: state which stop rule applies, using the one built-in gate that does stop for the human. Then make FR-19 and AC-19 say the same thing, and give the AC both cases (auto-approved and stopped).

sources.situation: an effort under auto reaches a passing extension gate. FR-19 says the driver approves it. AC-19 expects status "waiting on the human" and no agent pass line. A test written to AC-19 fails on a correct FR-19 implementation, and a correct AC-19 implementation breaks FR-19. AC-19 also says "that the flow's stop rules send to the human" without naming which rule or which gate, so the test has no concrete setup.

findings.reason: FR-19 says the driver's `nio flow done` approves a passing extension gate. AC-19 expects the flow to wait for the human at the step under auto. It names no rule or gate that makes the second case occur.
findings.note: Same fix as J-15: FR-19 and AC-19 now say the same thing, with both cases

findings.title: "Fails on its assertions, not on setup" has no observable
quotes: every such test fails on its assertions, not on setup
the check exits 0 with all tests failing on assertions
findings.fix: define the classification as a rule a test can check. For example, a failure counts as a feature failure only when the runner reports an assertion failure on a started app. Then give fixture cases for syntax error, import error, timeout and app down.

sources.situation: a Playwright test fails on a selector timeout or a 404 because the page route is missing. That is the feature missing. A test with a broken import fails before any assertion. A test whose `goto` hits a dead server also fails before any assertion. The spec never says how the check tells these apart (the runner's error type, an exit code, a report field). AC-31 only checks that "the output says the app didn't start". Two implementers would classify the same run differently, and nobody can write a fixture that must pass or must fail. The journey's "tests that fail because the app never started rather than because the feature is missing" has the same problem.

the tester writes `expect(true).toBe(false)` under a comment naming the AC. It cites its AC and fails on an assertion, so the check passes. A test that fails on a typo, a selector timeout, or a 500 page from a half-started app also counts as an assertion failure. UJ-4 lists "tests that fail because the app never started rather than because the feature is missing" as misuse, but AC-31 only separates a non-starting app. Nothing separates failing because the feature is missing from failing for any other reason.

findings.reason: FR-30 and AC-30 use "fails on its assertions, not on setup", and AC-31 covers only an app that doesn't start. No runner error class, exit code or report field is named to separate a selector timeout, an import error and a missing route.
findings.note: FR-41 and AC-45: a feature failure is a failed Playwright web-first assertion on a started app; syntax, import, timeout and page-free assertions fail the check

findings.title: NFR-1 to NFR-3 have no AC, Level or number
quotes: within its current speed limit (the `NIO_PERF=1` check) with three extensions added
300 seconds unless the manifest sets another, and record it as failed
leave the flow, history and status of an effort unchanged in a project with no extensions added
findings.fix: add one AC per NFR with an Observable and a Level. Say that the timeout value is settable by the manifest, so tests use a few seconds. Give a malformed-timeout case. Name the NFR-1 limit's value. Name the NFR-3 snapshot comparison.

sources.situation: no AC covers the hook or check timeout. Nobody can say whether a 300 s hook is killed, whether a manifest value is validated (0, negative, a string), or whether the failed record has the same shape as a non-zero exit. A real 300 s test is also impractical, and the spec doesn't say the timeout can be set small. NFR-1 refers to a limit by name only, so the number may change under it, and it doesn't say what the three extensions contain (steps, hooks, cards). NFR-3 has no baseline that "unchanged" is measured against, such as a golden snapshot.

findings.reason: NFR-1 to NFR-3 appear in no AC. NFR-1 refers to a limit only by name, NFR-2's timeout has no malformed-value or short-timeout case, and NFR-3 has no baseline for "unchanged".
findings.note: AC-46, AC-47, AC-48 cover NFR-1 to NFR-3; the timeout is settable to 1 second and a malformed one is refused

findings.title: FR-7's three extra behaviours have no AC
quotes: an effort sitting at it moves on to the next stage, and an effort past a replaced step is not sent back
findings.fix: add ACs for removing while an effort sits at the step, removing after it passed, and replacing after it passed. Each one names the stage and the history lines expected afterwards.

sources.situation: AC-7 only checks that the folder is gone and that `nio flow status` of an effort "before its spot" no longer lists the step. Take an effort that is sitting at the removed step. A broken implementation could leave it stuck, or crash `nio flow next` on an unknown stage, and AC-7 still passes. The same holds if an effort that already passed the step is sent back. Replacement via AC-4 has the same hole: no AC says a re-add of a changed step list leaves a passed effort where it is. History lines "stay as written" has no Observable either.

findings.reason: AC-7 checks only the folder removal and an effort before the step. No AC covers an effort at the step, an effort past it, a replace (AC-4 checks only one copy and the new version), or the history lines "staying as written".
findings.note: AC-44 covers removing at and past the step, replacing past it, and history lines unchanged

findings.title: No failure cases for the git and path sources
quotes: WHEN `nio extensions add` is given a git URL THE SYSTEM SHALL fetch the extension from it
findings.fix: add an AC for a failed fetch or missing path (non-zero exit, `.nio/extensions` unchanged, an earlier copy kept). Name the form of the recorded revision.

sources.situation: the URL is unreachable or needs credentials. The repo has no manifest. The path doesn't exist or is a file. The git binary is missing. Nothing says the add is refused, that nothing is half-copied, or that a previously added copy survives a failed re-add (FR-4). AC-5 covers only a bad manifest. A failed fetch could leave a half-written `.nio/extensions/<name>` and no test would catch it. "the version names the fetched revision" in AC-2 also doesn't say whether that is a commit hash, a tag or the manifest version, so the check isn't exact.

findings.note: a minor, accepted as the gate's risk under auto

findings.title: Replacing an extension while an effort sits at its step is not refused
quotes: it refuses the remove, naming the effort, while an effort sits at one of its steps
findings.fix: extend the FR-7 refusal to a replace that drops or renames a step an effort sits at, and add that case to AC-44.

sources.situation: an effort sits at step `s` of extension A. The maintainer re-adds A in a version without `s`. FR-7 and AC-44 case one refuse only `nio extensions remove`. AC-44 case two covers only an effort already past the step. FR-39 covers only another extension's `after`. So the effort sits at a step that no longer exists, and the spec gives no outcome. The effort could be stuck, or it could move on without the check or the gate.
